An implied forward rate is a break-even calculation: chart the reinvestment assumption

Distinguish one-year, two-year and forward rates, compare terminal cash values, reconcile reinvested interest and test the unknown second year in four charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two-year value with an unknown second-year reinvestment rate

Interactive planning lab

Implied one-year forward rate for year two6.01%
Two-year ending value: reinvest at the selected year-two rate$10,920
Reinvestment path minus two-year locked value-$105

Original two-year mathematical comparison, with independently selected annual effective rates and CAD capital. The two-year path pays capital × (1 + two-year spot rate)² at year two. The rolling path earns the selected one-year rate in year one, then reinvests the full receipt at the selected year-two rate. Neither path permits interim withdrawals in this calculation. An implied forward is the rate that makes their terminal values equal, not a forecast, a tradable forward quote, a product promise or a current market observation. Any market-pricing interpretation requires comparable currency, credit risk, dates and conventions. No fees, tax, inflation, default, borrowing, early sale or later rate change is modeled. Negative year-two rates are hypothetical value-decline stresses, not an available deposit quote.

The central idea

Two chosen spot rates imply a second-year rate that equalizes two-year values. That identity does not establish the return actually available when the first investment matures.

01

Compare the cash at one common two-year date

Imagine CAD 10,000 assigned to a payment due in two years. One hypothetical path uses a two-year annual effective rate of 5%, with the full amount paid at year two. The other earns 4% over one year, then reinvests the entire receipt for another year at a rate that is not yet known.

The first path’s assumed ending value is CAD 10,000 × 1.05² = CAD 11,025. The rolling path has CAD 10,400 at year one. What it has at year two depends on the return obtained for that second period.

The CFA Institute’s public term-structure overview explains that spot and forward rates refer to related periods. This original example turns that relationship into a cash comparison without using any actual bond or deposit quote.

02

Three annualized rates can describe three different intervals

The one-year spot rate covers today to year one. The two-year spot rate covers today to year two and is quoted here as an annual effective rate. Its two-year growth factor is therefore the square of one plus that rate.

The implied one-year forward rate covers only year one to year two. It is the second-year rate that makes the rolling path’s ending value equal to the two-year path’s value. It is neither a two-year cumulative return nor a rate for year three.

The first chart labels these periods beside the three percentages. A difference between two displayed yields does not by itself supply the forward rate. The comparison has to preserve the compounded growth factors over the same total horizon.

03

Solve the equality of growth factors

Let s1 be the one-year annual effective spot rate, s2 the two-year annual effective spot rate and f the one-year forward rate for the second year, all written as fractions. The matching condition is (1+s1)(1+f) = (1+s2)².

Solving gives f = (1+s2)² ÷ (1+s1) − 1. At the example’s rates, f = 1.05² ÷ 1.04 − 1, or approximately 6.00962% effective for year two.

Applied to CAD 10,400, that rate creates CAD 625 of second-year interest. The rolling path then reaches CAD 11,025, exactly matching the two-year path under the stated assumptions. The simple approximation 2 × 5% − 4% gives 6%; the exact compounded relation is slightly different.

04

The rate you actually obtain can fall on either side

The default second-year input is 5%, which is below the calculated break-even rate. CAD 10,400 then earns CAD 520 during year two and reaches CAD 10,920. That is CAD 105 less than the assumed two-year ending value.

The curve varies the second-year effective rate, while the starting amount and both original spot-rate inputs remain fixed. Its rising line is the rolling path’s terminal value. The horizontal comparison is the two-year path’s terminal value. Their intersection gives the break-even rate for positive capital, and the gold point identifies the selected second-year assumption.

A point above the comparison describes a higher two-year value for the rolling path under that rate. It does not establish that the rate will be available, that the two opportunities carry equivalent risk or that the household can make its payment after actual costs and taxes.

05

Reinvest the first year’s interest once

The waterfall starts with CAD 10,000, adds CAD 400 from year one and then adds the selected CAD 520 from year two. The endpoint is CAD 10,920. Year-two interest applies to all CAD 10,400 carried into that period.

Applying the second-year rate only to the original CAD 10,000 would leave out interest earned on the first year’s interest. Adding another CAD 400 as a separate contribution would count the earlier receipt twice.

The comparison assumes the full year-one amount can be reinvested immediately. Spending part of it, waiting before reinvesting or changing the payment date would alter the result. The separate two-year payoff is an alternative path and is never added to the rolling path as a second asset.

06

An implied forward does not guarantee the future market rate

The algebra identifies the reinvestment rate consistent with two chosen growth factors. It is not a prediction model. Actual future rates can be higher or lower, and different products can have different credit, liquidity, tax and access characteristics.

The Bank of England’s discussion of long-term rates distinguishes expectations about future short rates from term premia. That broader market context helps explain why a curve-derived rate should not automatically be read as a pure, certain forecast.

This calculator supplies no tradable forward contract. It also does not test whether an arbitrary pair of entered rates forms an available, arbitrage-free market curve. A market-pricing interpretation requires matching currencies, credit assumptions, dates and rate conventions; comparing unrelated retail offers would need further analysis.

07

A declining pair of spot rates can imply a negative forward

As a mathematical check, set the one-year spot rate to 8% and the two-year annual effective spot rate to 2%. The formula gives 1.02² ÷ 1.08 − 1, or about −3.67% for year two. Both entered spot rates are positive, while the calculated second-period rate is negative.

That follows because the first-year growth factor is already large relative to the selected two-year factor. It does not forecast negative deposit rates or verify that this combination of opportunities can actually be traded. The chart retains the sign so the calculation is not silently floored at zero.

The sensitivity range also allows a negative second-year return. Such a scenario reduces the value of the amount carried into that year. It is an independently selected stress, rather than a statement about a protected deposit or any actual provider’s terms.

08

Use the matrix to test the part of the plan that remains unknown

The matrix replaces the two-year annualized spot rate and the second-year reinvestment rate. It retains starting capital and the original one-year rate. Each cell shows rolling terminal value minus two-year terminal value, using the same two-year date.

The selected range can reveal when a plan depends on obtaining a strong renewal rate. It gives no probability for that outcome and does not evaluate credit quality, deposit protection or early access. Those questions remain separate from the matching equation.

  1. Write the amount and date of the goal.
  2. Convert both opportunities to consistent effective-rate and cash-flow conventions.
  3. Calculate the second-year rate needed to match their terminal values.
  4. Test lower and higher reinvestment outcomes.
  5. Check actual payment promises, costs, tax, access and provider terms before relying on the plan.

At zero starting capital, both dollar outcomes are zero at every rate. The spot-to-forward formula remains defined as a rate relationship, but the flat zero-value curves do not identify a unique cash break-even point. For a funded goal, the original capital and the reinvestment assumption both need a place in the plan.
